Indonesia Palm Oil: Production Revised Downward on Extreme Dryness

USDA estimates marketing year (MY) 2026/27 Indonesia palm oil production at 45.0 million
metric tons, down      5 percent from last month, and 4 percent from last year. Harvested area is
estimated at 14.0 million hectares, unchanged from last month and matching last year. Yield is
estimated at 3.21 tons per hectare, down 5 percent from last month, and 4 percent from last year.
























A prolonged dry spell has affected much of the palm oil production region since July, particularly
in eastern and southern Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces. Palm oil is predominantly dependent
on sufficient rainfall and soil moisture to ensure palm oil fruits can achieve optimal output. When
the necessary water levels, ranging from 150 to 200 millimeters monthly or 2,400 millimeters
annually, are not achieved, the reproductive cycle of the palm oil tree is adversely impacted.
Extended dry conditions lead to considerable tree stress and notable increases in the production of
male flowers     are apparent, while the development of female flowers decrease. This imbalance
hinders  effective  pollination,  ultimately  resulting  in  a  significant  reduction  in  the  yield  of
harvestable fruit.    Palm oil production is derived from the pressing of harvestable palm fruit
kernels.


                        Approved by the World Agricultural Outlook Board


=== PDF PAGE 2 ===
Additionally, in extreme dry cases, the vegetation or fronds on the palm oil tree would wither and
dry as to reduce further transpiration. This is a physiological response to conserve water, which
further exacerbates the negative impact on palm oil production. Local reports highlight extensive
observations of fronds withering in palm producing provinces on                   the island of Sumatra. The use
of  vegetative  response  indicators  through  assessing  both  the                 satellite-derived     Normalized
Difference Vegetative Index (NDVI) and Red-Edge Stress Vegetation Index validates the extent
of palm oil tree stress in the region. These observations convey less crop vegetative vigor or
greenness and are indicative to the extent of fronds withering as vegetative response signals are
not as high compared to last year.























Due to the magnitude of the observed dryness, Indonesia crude palm oil production is estimated
to decline from last year. Other prominent sources             , such as   the Indonesia Palm Oil Association           ,
has forecast its Indonesia crude palm oil production to decline up to 4 percent from last year.                    (For
more information, please contact Justin.Jenkins@usda.gov.)

China Peanuts: Production Declines              with Reduced Planted Area and Unfavorable Weather

USDA estimates China’s peanut production for marketing year 2026/27 at 18.0 million metric tons
(mmt), down 4 percent from last month, 2 percent from last year, and 4 percent below the five                      ‑year
average. Harvested area is estimated at 4.8 million hectares, down                 3 percent from last month and
3 percent from last year. Yield is estimated at 3.79 metric tons per hectare, down 1 percent from
last month but up 1 percent from last year.










=== PDF PAGE 3 ===
According to FAS/Beijing, lower production is primarily the result of reduced planted area in
major producing regions of the North China Plain and unfavorable weather during the growing
season. Planted area in these regions has been declining for several years due to poor net returns
and rising production costs, including fertilizer, land rent, and labor. As a result, some farmers
have shifted to alternative crops such as corn, sweet potatoes, and soybeans.


















=== PDF PAGE 4 ===
In mid‑August, Typhoon Dolphin brought heavy rainfall to key producing provinces in the North
China Plain - including Shandong, Henan, Anhui, and Hubei - during critical peanut growth stages.
Waterlogging in low‑lying areas hindered root development and further reduced yield potential.
Henan is China’s largest peanut-producing province, accounting for nearly one‑third of national
production and 28 percent of total planted area. Shandong ranks second, producing about 15
percent of the total crop. (For more information, contact Dath K. Mita at Dath.Mita@usda.gov.)

Canada Wheat: Above-Average Yield but Below Last Year’s Record

USDA estimates Canada wheat production for marketing year 2026/27 at 36.5 million metric tons,
up 1 percent from last month, down 10 percent from last year’s record, and up 9 percent from the
5-year average. Harvested area is estimated at 10.1 million hectares, unchanged from last month,
but down 5 percent from last year, and 2 percent below the 5-year average. Yield is estimated at
3.61 metric tons per hectare, up 1 percent from last month, down 5 percent from last year, but up
12 percent from the 5-year average.

Conditions this season brought favorable yields to most of the Prairies and more precipitation than
last year to Eastern Canada. Statistics Canada’s (StatCan) model-based field crop estimate based
on August agroclimatic and satellite data projected a 10.9 percent decrease from last year’s record
production since farmers planted less wheat and yields fell below last year’s record but remained
above the 5-year average.





=== PDF PAGE 5 ===
Spring wheat is predominantly grown in the Prairie provinces and accounts for approximately 96
percent of the total wheat crop.         In the Prairies, provincial reporting at the end of September
indicated that recent warm and dry weather allowed farmers to make significant harvest progress
despite below-average progress in Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba. Earlier in the harvest,
wet fields caused delays.       As of September 28, in Saskatchewan,               the  durum and spring wheat
harvest are 79 and 65 percent complete, respectively. This growing season, adequate soil moisture
supported average-to-above average vegetation conditions as seen in the satellite-derived Percent
of Average Seasonal Greenness (PASG) compared to the same period historically.































Winter wheat is predominantly grown in Ontario and comprises about 4 percent of total wheat.
Compared to last year’s widespread and severe drought, especially in the eastern region, this
season’s conditions were regionally variable, but overall beneficial precipitation supported slightly
above-average winter wheat yield prospects.

Spring wheat is often planted in late April to May in the Prairies and harvested in late August to
October.   Winter wheat is typically harvested in late July to early August, and this year was
completed earlier than last year. (For more information, please contact Sarah.Parker@usda.gov.)







=== PDF PAGE 6 ===
Mexico Wheat: Above-Average Temperatures Lower Winter Crop Yield

USDA estimates Mexico wheat production for marketing year (MY) 2026/27 at 1.9 million metric
tons (mmt), down 8 percent from last month, up 8 percent from last year’s drought-impacted crop,
but 37 percent below the 5-year average. Harvested area is estimated at 385,000 hectares, up 3
percent from last month and 25 percent from last year, but 22 percent below the 5-year average.
Yield is estimated at 4.81 metric tons per hectare, down 10 percent from last month and 14 percent
from last year.

Wheat in Mexico is predominantly grown in the fall/winter season, which accounts for about 96
percent of total production. Fall/winter wheat was planted from October through December 2025
and harvested from      April through July 2026. This crop season is almost entirely dependent on
irrigation. A partial recovery in reservoir levels in Sonora, the largest producing state, supported
farmers in sowing almost three times the area of last year’s drought impacted crop, according to
Mexico’s Agri-Food and Fisheries             Information Service (SIAP).          Despite enough water being
available to sufficiently irrigate the fall/winter crop, farmers in southern Sonora reported low
yields. Therefore, Mexico’s wheat was on track to have a decent recovery from the severe drought
until atypical weather prevented proper wheat grain development.























Fall/winter wheat requires a prolonged exposure to cold temperatures to trigger flowering once
warmer days  return, a  process  called vernalization.             This  fall/winter crop season,         minimum
temperatures  (red bars       in  above graphic) were insufficiently cold to  induce the shift  from
vegetative growth to reproductive growth for much of the crop in Sonora. Without enough cold
hours, the plant puts more energy into the green biomass instead of the grain, leading to poorer
yields.






=== PDF PAGE 7 ===
Satellite-derived  Normalized  Difference  Vegetation  Index  (NDVI)  measurements  show  less
vigorous green up as an indicator of the impacted yields. Mexico’s SIAP recently reported the
latest available fall/winter production estimate at 1.74 mmt, which is 7 percent greater than SIAP’s
final fall/winter and drought-impacted estimate for last year, yet still far below the 5-year average
of 3.08 mmt from 2020 to 2024. As a result, total production remains well below the 5-year
average.

While most of the wheat production in Mexico is irrigated and grown in the fall/winter season, the
remaining production       is mostly rainfed and is planted in the spring/summer season from April
through July and harvested from September through December. (For more information, please
contact Lisa.Colson@usda.gov.)

Turkey Wheat: Production Raised to a New Record

USDA estimates Turkey’s wheat production for marketing year 2026/27 at a record 23.0 million
metric tons, up 2 percent from last month, 37 percent above last year’s drought-affected crop, and
28  percent  above  the  5-year  average.  Harvested  area  is  estimated  at  7.5  million  hectares,
unchanged from last month, but up 2 percent from last year. Yield is estimated at a record 3.09
tons per hectare, 2 percent above last month, 34 percent above last year, and 22 percent above the
5-year average.









=== PDF PAGE 8 ===
Turkey, along with much of the Middle East and North Africa region, received well above-average
rainfall this year. After steep production declines across the region last year due to drought, this
season brought drought-breaking rains. Above-average precipitation and moderate temperatures
created highly favorable conditions, boosting yields throughout the Middle East. In Turkey, these
conditions   supported a larger-than-expected wheat harvest, raising production to a new record.
(For more information, please contact Bryan.Purcell@usda.gov.)



=== PDF PAGE 9 ===
Philippines Rice: Extended Dryness Decreases Production

USDA estimates Philippines          rice production     for marketing year (MY)          2026/27 at 12.1     million
metric tons (milled basis), down 2 percent from last month and from last year. Harvested area is
estimated at 4.6 million hectares, down 2 percent from last month and 3 percent from last year.
Yield (rough basis) is estimated at 4.18 tons per hectare, down less than 1 percent from last month
but up 1 percent from last year.

USDA’s marketing year for Philippines rice begins in July and ends in June the following calendar
year. The marketing        year begins with Quarter 3, which accounts for 19 percent of national
production. Quarterly output is reported by the Philippine Statistical Authority (PSA).





























Rice cultivation in the Philippines occurs throughout the year and                   is  primarily dependent       on
seasonal weather for optimal yields. The sowing period for rice follows a seasonal rainfall pattern
comprised of a wet season, from June to November, followed by a dry season, from December to
May. Cumulative rainfall observed during the onset of the wet season trended below-average, most
notably in Western Visayas, Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley and Central Luzon, where rice is
predominantly sown during Quarter 3. As a result, limited water availability delayed sowing
operations for up to 2 weeks for some farmers.





=== PDF PAGE 10 ===
According to observations from FAS/Manila and FAS/Washington in early August 2026, fields
that were cultivated had accessibility to water resources through usage of well pumps, solar sub-
pumps, or river access. However, with reductions to the water table due to insufficient rains in
some areas,    the pumps became         useless, most notably in the northern Cagayan Valley region.
Welcomed rainfall accumulations brought relief to the regions, driven by Tropical Depression
MayMay observed in early August. However, rainfall through mid-September had mixed results
as much of the region had experienced average to below-average rainfall. In response to the
growing conditions and weather, the PSA preliminary report on rice production for Quarter 3 was
down 15 percent from the same period last year. Consequently,                    harvested rice    area was also
reported down 16 percent from the same period last year. Quarter 4 harvesting period has begun
and extends through December and attributes roughly 36 percent of the national production total.
(For more information, please contact Justin.Jenkins@usda.gov.)

Argentina Corn: MY 2025/26 Favorable Seasonal Conditions Boost Yield

USDA estimates Argentina          corn production for marketing year (MY) 2025/26 at a record 64.0
million metric tons, up 2 percent from last month and 31 percent from MY 2024/25. Corn yield is
estimated at 7.80 tons per hectare, up 2 percent from last month, and 9 percent from MY 2024/25.
Harvested area is estimated at a record 8.2 million hectares (mha), unchanged from last month, but
up 20 percent from MY 2024/25.


































=== PDF PAGE 11 ===
Planting for the MY 2025/26 crop occurred from September 2025 until February 2026. Argentina
farmers plant both early-planted corn (corn planted prior to December 1st) and late-planted corn
(corn planted after December 1st). In an average year, early corn is about 2.5 mha, but early corn
planted area for the last two marketing years of MY 2024/25 and MY 2025/26 was around 3.0
mha. Farmers planted more early corn in the last two seasons because early planted corn largely
missed the chicharrita (leafhopper) infestation that occurred in 2023.
During January and early February 2026, there were below normal rainfall conditions. According
to Bolsa Cereales Buenos Aires, however, most of the early corn had already passed the critical
yield development stage and only a portion of the late corn was in that phase during that window.
Most of the late corn crop went through the critical yield phase once rainfall returned during
February. Other than this brief period of dryness, the weather over the growing season was
favorable.
Corn harvest usually begins at the end of March and continues through the end of August. This
year, however, corn harvest was delayed due to excessive rainfall. The corn harvest for MY
2025/26 finally concluded towards the end of September, overlapping the corn planting for MY
2026/27. Corn harvest results were higher-than-normal in the main corn growing regions. (For
more information, please contact Katie.McGaughey@usda.gov)
Mexico Sorghum: Erratic Weather Patterns Limit Area

USDA estimates Mexico sorghum production for marketing year (MY) 2026/27                             at 3.6 million
metric tons (mmt), down 13 percent from last month, up 6 percent from last year, but down 18
percent from the 5-year average. Harvested area is estimated at 1.1                  million hectares, down 13
percent from last month, up 5 percent from last year, and 17 percent below the 5-year average.
Yield is estimated at 3.43 tons per hectare, down 1 percent from last month, but up 1 percent last
year. Farmers made decisions to plant less          area to sorghum as they struggle with profitability and
El Niño related weather impacts that keep area near a similar 30             -year low as last year.

Mexico sorghum is        produced in     two seasons,     with   spring/summer      covering approximately 45
percent of the total and then         fall/winter   covering the remaining 55 percent            . Spring/summer
sorghum is typically planted from           March    through    August.   Mexico’s Agri-Food and Fisheries
Information Service (SIAP) reported the latest available planted area estimate at 310,000 hectares,
which is 28 percent below SIAP’s planted area estimate for the MY 2025/26 spring/summer crop.
Farmers struggle with low crop prices, high farmer debt, limited access to credit and government
support, and erratic precipitation patterns. According to SIAP, planting in                 Guanajuato, which is
the largest producer for the spring/summer crop, was reduced by 14 percent due to the crop’s lack
of profitability. Harvest has already begun on approximately 10 percent of               the spring/summer crop.












=== PDF PAGE 12 ===
In late September, FAS/Washington and FAS/Mexico City conducted a crop condition assessment
in Jalisco. While the state accounts for about 7 percent of spring/summer sorghum, Jalisco is
typically the fourth largest producer. In Jalisco, average to above-average sorghum crop conditions
were observed, supporting average yields.






























=== PDF PAGE 13 ===
The fall/winter sorghum is typically planted from September through March, but planting will be
delayed until October this year because of dryness. FAS/Mexico City reported low planting
intentions by farmers in Tamaulipas, where 77 percent of fall/winter sorghum is produced. Starting
in mid-August, soil moisture has been below average in the state. The monthly precipitation record
since 1981 shows that September 2026 has been the driest September in 45 years in northern
Tamaulipas, according to CHIRPS precipitation rank. The reductions in area for both seasons
resulted   in   a   decline   in   total   production.         (For   more   information,   please   contact
Lisa.Colson@usda.gov.)

European Union Corn: Poor Weather Drives Yield and Production Down Further

USDA estimates European Union (EU) corn production for marketing year (MY) 2026/27 at 48.0
million metric tons (mmt), down          5 percent from last month, 16 percent from last year, and 21
percent below the 5-year average. This is the smallest crop since MY 1994/95, when the bloc had
fewer member states. Harvested area is estimated at 7.4 million hectares (mha), down 1 percent
from last month and 10 percent from last year, marking the lowest harvested area on record. Yield
is estimated at 6.52 tons per hectare, down 4 percent from last month, 6 percent from last year, and
7 percent below the 5-year average, and is the lowest since MY 2022/23.



































=== PDF PAGE 14 ===
France and Hungary were severely affected by extreme summer heat and dryness. France, typically
the EU’s leading corn producer—by a wide margin—was surpassed this year by both Poland and
Romania,     following  more  favorable  weather  in  those  countries.  USDA  estimates  France’s
production at 7.0 mmt, down 1.5 mmt from last month, the lowest output in 50 years. Harvested
area in France is estimated at 1.2 mha, the smallest in 58 years.




























Hungary’s crop was similarly reduced. Production is estimated at 2.1 mmt, the lowest in USDA’s
series on Hungary dating to 1960. Harvested area, at 0.6 mha, is also a record low. Germany’s
production is reduced by 0.4 mmt this month to 4.1 mmt following the release of official statistics.
Much of southern Germany was mired in a prolonged drought during the summer growing season.
Harvest is ongoing across Europe, particularly in France, where the crop was nearing 50 percent
complete by the end of September.

For country-specific area, yield, and production estimates within the EU, please go to PSD Online
at  https://apps.fas.usda.gov/PSDOnline/app/index.html#/app/home,  and  select  “Downloadable
Data Sets.” Select the zipped file for “EU Countries Area & Production.” (For more information,
please contact Bryan.Purcell@usda.gov.)










=== PDF PAGE 15 ===
Brazil Cotton: Record Yield Offsets Year-to-Year Area Reduction

USDA     estimates Brazil      cotton   production for marketing year          (MY)    2026/27     at a record 19.0
million 480-pound bales, up 3 percent from last month, 1 percent from last year and 30 percent
above the 5-year average. Harvested area is estimated at 2.0 million hectares, unchanged from last
month, but down 4 percent from last year, yet 15 percent above the 5-year average. Yield is
estimated at a record 2,068 kilograms per hectare, up 3 percent from last month, 6 percent from
last year, and 14 percent above the 5-year average.


























Brazil estimates another cotton production record for MY 2026/27, as record yields offset reduced
planted area. Tighter margins and increased national interest in safrinha corn led to lower planted
area, particularly in Mato Grosso, which produces over 70 percent of Brazil’s cotton. The Mato
Grosso Institute for Agricultural Economics (IMEA) reports a year-to-year reduction in harvested
area of 11 percent. However, seasonal conditions were ideal, boosting yields, and IMEA reports a
record yield in Mato Grosso that is 3 percent higher than last year.














=== PDF PAGE 16 ===
Conditions were also highly favorable in Bahia, where planted area held relatively steady and
yields rose 6 percent from last year, according to the September report by the Companhia Nacional
de Abastecimento (CONAB). Irrigated cotton now accounts for roughly 44 percent of Bahia’s total
cotton area, based on estimates from Agroconsult. Although irrigated fields typically outperform
rainfed areas, Agroconsult observed in its recent crop tour reporting that many rainfed areas in
Bahia matched or even exceeded irrigated yields this season. These strong rainfed yields were key
in offsetting national area reductions and supported overall production. (For more information,
please contact Aaron.Mulhollen@usda.gov.)

The Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) updates its production, supply and distribution (PSD)
database for cotton, oilseeds, and grains at 12:00 p.m. on the day the World Agricultural Supply
and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report is released.  This circular is released by 12:15 p.m.

                                               FAS Reports and Databases:

World Agricultural Production
Current:   https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/world-agricultural-production
Archive:  https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/publication/world-agricultural-production
USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) publishes a monthly report on crop acreage, yield and production in major
countries  worldwide.  Sources  include  reporting  from            FAS’s     worldwide  offices,  official  statistics  of  foreign
governments, and analysis of economic data and satellite imagery. The reports reflect official USDA estimates
released in the monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE).

World Markets and Trade
Current:   https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/search?reports%5B0%5D=report_type%3A10259
Archive:  https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/?f%5B0%5D=agency%3A1
USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) publishes monthly and quarterly reports which include data on U.S. and
global trade, production, consumption and stocks, as well as analysis of developments affecting world trade in
oilseeds, grains, cotton, livestock and poultry. The reports reflect official USDA estimates released in the monthly
World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE).

Global Agricultural Information Network (GAIN)
https://gain.fas.usda.gov/
USDA's  Foreign  Agricultural  Service  (FAS)  provides  timely  reports  on  foreign  markets  through  the  Global
Agriculture Information Network (GAIN) database. An average of 2,000 reports are added each year, with reports
going back to 1995. GAIN reports are compiled by FAS’ global market intelligence network, which includes FAS
foreign service officers and locally engaged staff in over 90 overseas offices world-wide. They provide on-the-ground
intelligence, insight, and analysis on nearly 200 countries, delivering information on foreign agricultural markets, crop
conditions,  and  agro-political  dynamics  of  interest  to  U.S.  agriculture.  GAIN  reports  contain  assessments  of
commodity and trade issues made by USDA staff and are not necessarily statements of official U.S. government
policy.
Production, Supply and Distribution (PS&D) Online
https://apps.fas.usda.gov/psdonline/app/index.html#/app/home
PSD Online is the public repository for USDA’s Official Production, Supply and Distribution forecast data and reports
for key agricultural commodities. PSD Online data are reviewed and updated monthly by an interagency committee
chaired by USDA’s World Agricultural Outlook Board (WAOB). The committee consist of representatives from
Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS), the Economic Research Service (ERS), the Farm Service Agency (FSA), and the
Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS).

EU Countries and Russia Wheat: Area and Production Estimates
https://apps.fas.usda.gov/psdonline/app/index.html#/app/downloads  (click on PSD Datasets)
USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) provides country-level area and production estimates for the nations of
the European Union. For Russia, country-level area and production estimates are provided for Winter and Spring
wheat. These datasets are reviewed and updated monthly by an interagency committee chaired by USDA’s World
Agricultural Outlook Board (WAOB) and can be downloaded through PSD datasets on PSD Online.








=== PDF PAGE 20 ===
                                               FAS Reports and Databases:


International Production Assessment (IPAD)
Due to U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) guidance, the International Production Assessment Division (IPAD)
website is no longer available to the public. Crop production maps, crop calendars, and historical commodity-specific
area, yield, and production data is available on the FAS website.
https://www.fas.usda.gov/data

USDA and NASA Global Agricultural Monitoring (GLAM)
https://glam1.gsfc.nasa.gov/
The USDA and NASA Global Agricultural Monitoring (GLAM) system provides near real-time and science quality
Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from
the satellites Terra and Aqua. The public can view and retrieve MODIS 8-day composited, global NDVI satellite
imagery and time series data. GLAM was developed by NASA’s Global Inventory Modeling and Mapping Studies
(GIMMS) group for USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service.

Global Agricultural and Disaster Assessment System (GADAS)
https://geo.fas.usda.gov/GADAS/index.html
USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) provides the Global Agricultural and Disaster Assessment System
(GADAS), a web-based Geographic Information System (GIS) tool which integrates a vast array of highly detailed
earth observation data streams, particularly targeted towards agricultural and disaster assessment analysis. GADAS is
an interactive website which provides analysts with a wide variety of routine geospatial products (maps, charts, tables)
they require for comprehensive situational investigations and recurring assessments.

Export Sales Reporting
https://apps.fas.usda.gov/esrquery/
USDA’s Export Sales Reporting Program monitors U.S. agricultural export sales on a daily and weekly basis. Export
sales reporting provides a constant stream of up-to-date market information for 40 U.S. agricultural commodities sold
abroad. The weekly U.S. Export Sales report is the most currently available source of U.S. exports sales data. The data
is used to analyze overall levels of export demand, determine where markets exit, and assess the relative position of
U.S. commodities in foreign markets.

Global Agricultural Trade System (GATS)
https://apps.fas.usda.gov/gats/default.aspx
The Global Agricultural Trade System (GATS) is a searchable database containing monthly U.S. Census Bureau trade
data organized by agricultural commodity and agricultural related product groups. Trade data is searchable by partner
countries and partner groups. Historical U.S. agricultural trade data is available back to 1967. In addition, U.N. trade
statistics (UN Comtrade) may be queried through GATS. UN trade data is available for nearly 200 countries or areas,
dating from the inception of the Harmonized              System (HS) of trade codes in 1989 to present. The database is
continuously updated. U.S. trade data is updated monthly according to the U.S. Census Bureau’s reporting system.
UN Comtrade data are updated in GATS after nationally submitted data to the UN                         are standardized by the UN
Statistical Division and added to the UN Comtrade database.
